## In 60 seconds

A mapping system knows activation times only where it recorded them; the colored **activation map** in between is
**interpolated**. Linear interpolation on a triangulation is exact for linear fields, and its error grows as the
square of the point spacing times the curvature of the activation pattern. **Inverse-distance weighting** never
overshoots, but for powers above 1 its gradient vanishes at every point, leaving flat bull's-eyes that make conduction
look fast. **Harmonic interpolation** on the mesh solves Laplace's equation between the points. It reproduces linear
fields when the boundary is fixed, but treats a free edge as if nothing crossed it. **Isochrones**, lines of equal
time, are $c\,\Delta\tau$ apart, so crowding signals slow conduction. Interpolation cannot represent a **line of
block**: it turns a jump into a ramp that reads as conduction at spacing over delay. Finally, a map is colored only
within a **fill threshold** of some point, and the colored fraction depends on point density.

## From the field

- **How many points are enough.** In simulations and 21 clinical atrial tachycardia maps, the sampling density beyond
  which re-interpolated maps improved little was about 1.0–1.5 points/cm² overall. It was higher for reentry than
  for focal activation, and higher in the complex left atrium [@williams2018].
- **Isochrone crowding as a target.** One registry defined deceleration zones as more than 3 isochrones within a 1-cm
  radius on sinus-rhythm maps annotated to the latest deflection. In 120 patients they colocalized with VT termination
  sites in 95% of cases, as the study reports [@aziz2019].
- **Display settings change the map.** Early descriptions of electroanatomic mapping already listed the triangle fill
  threshold and color range among display controls [@marchlinski1998]. Ripple mapping, which shows each electrogram
  as a moving bar instead of an interpolated color, was designed to overcome limitations of isochronal maps
  [@koawing2015].

## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** $T$ activation time; $T_i$ at mapped point $i$; $h$ point spacing; $\lambda_i$
barycentric weights; $d_i$ distance to point $i$; $p$ IDW power; $L$ cotangent Laplacian (m06); $\tau$ isochrone time;
$\Delta\tau$ isochrone step; $c$ conduction velocity; $\Delta T$ delay across a block; $\rho$ point density; $r$ fill
radius.

### Linear interpolation

Inside a triangle, $T(\mathbf x) = \sum_i \lambda_i(\mathbf x)\,T_i$ with barycentric weights. Along a line of points
spaced $h$:

$$
T(\mathbf x) = \sum_{i=1}^{3}\lambda_i(\mathbf x)\,T_i, \qquad \lvert T - I_h T\rvert \le \frac{h^2}{8}\max\lvert T''\rvert
$$ {#eq-m24-linear}

Linear fields are reproduced exactly; error comes from curvature. A focal activation is most curved near its source.
5 mm from a source at 1.0 m/s [@heil2023], points 5 mm apart gave a largest error of 0.45 ms against a bound of
0.63 ms (lab part A).

### Inverse-distance weighting

$$
T(\mathbf x) = \frac{\sum_i d_i^{-p}\,T_i}{\sum_i d_i^{-p}}, \qquad \min_i T_i \le T \le \max_i T_i, \qquad \nabla T(\mathbf x_i) = \mathbf 0 \text{ for } p > 1
$$ {#eq-m24-idw}

Shepard introduced the method [@shepard1968]; m30 uses it. Near a data point the point's own weight dominates, so for
$p > 1$ the map is flat there: a bull's-eye. In the lab, with 60 points, the median gradient near points was 0.41 ms/mm
for $p = 2$ and 0.02 ms/mm for $p = 3$, against a true 1.0 ms/mm. A speed computed from such a gradient (m25) is
inflated (lab part B).

::: {.demo #m24-d2 badge="simulation"}
```{=html}
<div id="m24-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m24-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m24-d2-isochrones.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: focal activation from one point in a uniform 40 × 40 mm sheet; points placed at random with a fixed seed;
  inverse-distance weighting on a 61 × 61 grid (@eq-m24-idw); isochrones by marching squares (@eq-m24-isochrone).
  Tested against `epml.interpolation`.
- Parameters: conduction velocity 1.0 m/s [@heil2023]; number of points, power and isochrone step are adjustable.
- What it ignores: annotation and position errors (m22, m16–m19), curved surfaces, block and slow regions.
:::

### Harmonic interpolation on a mesh

$$
(L\,T)_j = 0 \text{ at unmapped vertices } j, \qquad T_i \text{ fixed at mapped vertices } i
$$ {#eq-m24-harmonic}

This uses the cotangent Laplacian of m06 ([eq-m06-cotan](m06-meshes-geodesics.qmd#eq-m06-cotan)). The solution
never exceeds the data range (maximum principle), and on a flat mesh with the boundary fixed it reproduces linear
fields exactly. A free boundary, such as a valve or vein opening in a chamber mesh, acts as a zero-flux condition.
The map then bends isochrones to meet the edge at right angles. In the lab, a plane wave at 1.0 ms/mm gradient read
$-0.01$ ms/mm along the edge normal with a free edge, against 1.00 with the edge fixed. Harmonic maps from 200 points had
less than half the RMS error of IDW maps (lab part C).

### Isochrones

On a mesh with linear interpolation, the isochrone at time $\tau$ crosses edge $(i, j)$ at

$$
\mathbf x = \mathbf x_i + \frac{\tau - T_i}{T_j - T_i}(\mathbf x_j - \mathbf x_i), \qquad \text{spacing between isochrones } \Delta x = c\,\Delta\tau
$$ {#eq-m24-isochrone}

Crowded isochrones mean slow conduction or block, and widely spaced ones fast conduction. Isochronal late activation
maps use crowding to find deceleration zones [@aziz2019]. The spacing also depends on the step chosen for display.

### Block and coverage

Two points $h$ apart on either side of a line of block, activated $\Delta T$ apart, are joined by a ramp; a map of
$\rho$ randomly placed points colored within a fill radius $r$ covers a fraction:

$$
c_{\text{apparent}} = \frac{h}{\Delta T}, \qquad f_{\text{covered}} = 1 - e^{-\rho\pi r^2}
$$ {#eq-m24-block}

With points 4 mm apart whose activation times differ by 60 ms, the ramp reads 0.07 m/s: apparent slow conduction where nothing conducts (lab
part E). Denser points make the ramp steeper but never vertical. With 150 points on a 50 × 50 mm patch (6 per cm²) and a
3-mm fill radius, 82% of the patch is colored.

::: {.demo #m24-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m24-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m24-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m24-d1-block.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: activation along a line at constant speed with a single jump at a line of block; points sampled evenly,
  offset by half the spacing; linear interpolation and IDW on the sampled values (@eq-m24-linear,
  @eq-m24-idw, @eq-m24-block). Tested against `epml.interpolation`.
- Parameters: conduction velocity 1.0 m/s [@heil2023]; spacing, detour delay and IDW power are illustrative and
  adjustable.
- What it ignores: annotation of double potentials at the block (m22), noise, and the second dimension.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Interpolation fills in what was not measured; its errors depend on the method and the activation pattern.
- A ramp across a block and a flat spot at a point are both artifacts of interpolation, not physiology.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where this shows up in EP.** Every activation map shown during a procedure is interpolated. Sampling density needs
depend on how complex activation is [@williams2018]. Isochrone crowding has been used to identify deceleration zones
[@aziz2019]. Interpolation settings and display thresholds change what a map shows [@marchlinski1998], and displays
that show the electrograms themselves were designed to overcome limitations of isochronal maps [@koawing2015].

**What the evidence is.** A combined simulation and clinical study of sampling density [@williams2018], a prospective
registry [@aziz2019], descriptions of mapping displays [@marchlinski1998; @koawing2015], and interpolation theory
[@shepard1968].

**What a reader should ask:**

- **Which interpolation method, and does it flatten around points?** (@eq-m24-linear, @eq-m24-idw)
- **Are open edges handled, or do isochrones bend to meet them?** (@eq-m24-harmonic)
- **Is a crowded region slow conduction or interpolation across block?** (@eq-m24-isochrone, @eq-m24-block)
- **How dense are the points, and what fill threshold is set?** (@eq-m24-block) [@williams2018]

## How experts think

Before reading an activation map, ask:

1. **Where are the actual points?** Show them. (@eq-m24-block)
2. **Which interpolant, and what does it do near points and edges?** (@eq-m24-idw, @eq-m24-harmonic)
3. **Is the activation pattern curved where points are sparse?** (@eq-m24-linear)
4. **Is crowding real slowing, or a block smeared by interpolation?** (@eq-m24-isochrone, @eq-m24-block)
5. **Would a different fill threshold change the conclusion?** (@eq-m24-block)

One sentence to keep: **between the points, the map shows the interpolant, not the heart.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Linear (@eq-m24-linear) | $\sum\lambda_i T_i$; error $\le h^2\max\lvert T''\rvert/8$ |
| IDW (@eq-m24-idw) | $\sum d_i^{-p}T_i/\sum d_i^{-p}$; bounded; flat at points for $p > 1$ |
| Harmonic (@eq-m24-harmonic) | $L T = 0$ between points; free edges act as zero flux |
| Isochrones (@eq-m24-isochrone) | edge crossing $(\tau - T_i)/(T_j - T_i)$; spacing $c\,\Delta\tau$ |
| Block, coverage (@eq-m24-block) | apparent $h/\Delta T$; covered $1 - e^{-\rho\pi r^2}$ |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Optimal sampling about 1.0–1.5 points/cm² | @williams2018 |
| Deceleration zone: more than 3 isochrones within 1 cm; colocalized in 95% (120 patients) | @aziz2019 |
| Conduction velocity 1.0 m/s | @heil2023 |
| Point counts, delays, fill radii, source positions | illustrative |
| Errors, gradients, apparent speeds, coverage | our own code |

## Practice questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In your answer, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. What does a mapping system show between mapped points?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

An interpolated value; the choice of interpolant shapes the map (@eq-m24-linear, @eq-m24-idw, @eq-m24-harmonic).

</details>

**Q2. Bound the error of linear interpolation along a line.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$h^2\max\lvert T''\rvert/8$; it is exact for linear fields and worst where activation curves, near a focal
source (@eq-m24-linear).

</details>

**Q3. Why does IDW produce bull's-eyes?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

For $p > 1$ the nearest point's weight dominates so strongly that the gradient vanishes at every data
point (@eq-m24-idw) [@shepard1968].

</details>

**Q4. What does that do to conduction velocity maps?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Speed is the inverse of the gradient magnitude, so flat spots read as very fast conduction (@eq-m24-idw); m25 covers
estimators that avoid this.

</details>

**Q5. What is harmonic interpolation, and what is its advantage?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Solving $L T = 0$ between mapped vertices on the mesh; it follows the surface, cannot overshoot, and reproduces linear
fields with a fixed boundary (@eq-m24-harmonic).

</details>

**Q6. What happens at an open edge of the mesh?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It behaves as zero flux: isochrones bend to meet the edge at right angles, whatever the true
activation (@eq-m24-harmonic).

</details>

**Q7. How far apart are isochrones?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$c\,\Delta\tau$ for a front at speed $c$ and step $\Delta\tau$ (@eq-m24-isochrone).

</details>

**Q8. A map shows crowded isochrones. Name two explanations.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Slow conduction, or interpolation across a line of block, which turns a jump into a steep ramp (@eq-m24-block).

</details>

**Q9. Points 4 mm apart straddle a block, and their activation times differ by 60 ms. What speed does a linear map
show?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

4/60 ≈ 0.07 mm/ms, i.e. 0.07 m/s (@eq-m24-block).

</details>

**Q10. How many points does a map need?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It depends on activation complexity and geometry; one study found about 1.0–1.5 points/cm² beyond which maps improved
little [@williams2018]. m26 goes further.

</details>

**Q11. What fraction of a surface is colored for random points of density ρ and fill radius r?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$1 - e^{-\rho\pi r^2}$ (@eq-m24-block).

</details>

**Q12. How were deceleration zones defined in one VT study?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

More than 3 isochrones within a 1-cm radius on isochronal late activation maps [@aziz2019].

</details>

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. Halve the point spacing. What happens to the linear-interpolation error bound?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

It falls to a quarter (@eq-m24-linear).

</details>

**S2. Three points with times 10, 20, 30 ms. Can IDW return 35 ms anywhere?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

No; it stays within 10–30 ms (@eq-m24-idw).

</details>

**S3. Speed 0.5 m/s, isochrone step 10 ms. Isochrone spacing?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

5 mm (@eq-m24-isochrone).

</details>

**S4. An edge from 12 ms to 20 ms. Where does the 14-ms isochrone cross it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

A quarter of the way along (@eq-m24-isochrone).

</details>

**S5. Points 2 mm apart across a block, activation times 100 ms apart. Apparent speed?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

0.02 m/s (@eq-m24-block).

</details>

**S6. One point per cm², fill radius 5 mm. Covered fraction?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$1 - e^{-\pi/4} \approx$ 0.54 (@eq-m24-block).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Re-interpolated maps at falling density.** Williams and colleagues' maps and error curves against sampling density
  [@williams2018]. This module: block and coverage.
- **Isochronal crowding.** Aziz and colleagues' isochronal late activation maps with deceleration zones [@aziz2019].
  This module: isochrones.
- **Shepard's surfaces.** Shepard's interpolated surfaces for different powers [@shepard1968]. This module: inverse-
  distance weighting.

## Further reading

- **Interpolation.** Shepard's method [@shepard1968]; LAT and conduction-velocity algorithms [@cantwell2015]; the OpenEP
  platform [@williams2021].
- **Sampling.** Density for atrial tachycardia maps [@williams2018].
- **Clinical use of isochrones.** Deceleration zones [@aziz2019]; electrograms shown as moving bars [@koawing2015].
- **Related modules.** m06 (meshes), m22 (annotation), m25 (conduction velocity), m26 (map quality), m30 (capstone).
